extracted.intended_audience: legislators, political philosophers, and students of political theory (those concerned with founding and organising a city/polis)
extracted.subtask_description: Prescriptive guidance for constituting, organising, and educating a city-state so that its citizens can be happy and virtuous. Covers necessary institutions, land and property regimes, urban siting and defences, public architecture, civic virtue and education, marriage and childbearing norms, and the proper ends of legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constituent necessities of a city/state
rubrics_metrics.description: A city requires certain absolutely necessary parts: provision for internal order and defence (those who might refuse obedience and those who would attack from without); a revenue for internal necessities and the business of war; a religious establishment; and a court to determine both criminal and civil causes. Also necessary are husbandmen (to procure food), artificers, soldiers, rich men, priests and judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These elements are 'absolutely necessary' so that the city can secure independence and self-protection. If any of these essentials is wanting, the ends of the city cannot be obtained. The list functions as a checklist for what institutions and social roles must exist in any viable polis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allocation of occupations and civic eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Decide which employments are open to all citizens versus appropriated to particular classes: in the best-governed states, citizens should not exercise mechanic employment or follow merchandise as these are 'ignoble and destructive to virtue'; citizens should be free from husbandry so they may have leisure to 'improve in virtue' and perform duties to the state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ruling citizens ought to hold the more honourable offices (soldier, senator, judge) and to be landowners; manual or mercantile occupations should be performed by non-citizens (slaves, servants, barbarians). Where multiple functions require different abilities (courage vs judgment) they should be assigned to different persons; where those with arms may insist on power, combine offices as nature directs (young: courage; old: judgment).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property regime and land division
rubrics_metrics.description: The land ought to be divided into two broad parts — one belonging to the community (public) and the other to individuals — each of which should be further subdivided: half of the public portion to maintain worship of the gods, the other half to support common meals; half of individual holdings near the city, half at the extremity so each person partakes of both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This scheme aims for equality, harmony in war (shared stake in borders and interior), and public provisioning. Husbandmen who cultivate private property should belong to the individual owner; those who cultivate public territory should belong to the public. The text rejects full communal property but prescribes public arrangements to prevent want.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public provisioning and common meals
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Common meals' (communal dining) are proper in well-regulated cities; all citizens ought to partake. Religious worship expenses should be defrayed by the whole state; poor citizens may need public support because they cannot both contribute to common tables and supply their private household.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Common meals function as social and civic institutions promoting equality and cohesion. The legislator must provide for the poor and appropriate resources (from public land) to fund communal dining and cultic expenses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of non-citizen labour for agriculture
rubrics_metrics.description: Husbandmen ideally should be slaves (not of the same nation) or barbarians/servants so they will be industrious and unlikely to attempt novelties; those who cultivate private lands belong to the individual, those who cultivate public lands belong to the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This recommendation separates citizens from manual agricultural labour to preserve leisure and virtue among citizens. The legislator should make arrangements for the origin, status, and promises (e.g., liberty as reward) of such labourers; specifics of treatment are to be determined later.

rubrics_metrics.name: Urban site selection: health, defence, access, and water supply
rubrics_metrics.description: Four desiderata for city position: (1) health (cities facing east, then north, are most healthful), (2) proper situation for government and defence (easy access for citizens, difficult for enemies), (3) access/communication with sea and continent, (4) abundance of water — rivers or very large cisterns — with drinking water separated from other uses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Health and water are primary because air and water influence bodily health. Defensive siting must balance accessibility for citizens with difficulty of access for enemies. If natural water is lacking, store rainwater; in wise governments waters are appropriated to different uses and qualities are distinguished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fortifications and urban form for safety and ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: Walls, bulwarks, and towers are necessary in many cases; their form should suit the constitution (a lofty citadel for monarchy/oligarchy; a plain for democracy; many strong places for aristocracy). Walls should be both defence and ornament, incorporating modern improvements and proper towers at distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejects antiquated contempt for walls: practical defence (especially against siege machines) justifies fortifications. Private houses should include both detached 'modern' plans (per Hippodamus) for elegance and separated, labyrinthine forms suitable for wartime safety — the city should possess both types in different quarters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public building placement and squares organisation
rubrics_metrics.description: Temples and the hall for public tables of chief magistrates should be contiguous and conspicuous; there should be a large 'Square of Freedom' where buying and selling is forbidden (no mechanics or husbandmen may enter unless ordered), and a separate market square situated for goods received by sea and land. Priests' public tables near temples; magistrates' public tables near markets and courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spatial ordering reflects social hierarchies and civic functions: sacred, leisurely, and commercial/administrative spaces are distinct. Public ornament and the visibility of elders and magistrates performing exercises are used to inspire modesty and civic virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Composition of government: ends and means must align
rubrics_metrics.description: Excellence of government depends on two things: a proper end (the happiness of citizens) and means adapted to achieve it. The legislator must ensure that means (laws, education, institutions) are fit to procure the stated end; good ends with bad means or vice versa produce failure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Happiness is defined (drawing on Nicomachean ethics) as 'energy and perfect practice of virtue.' Therefore laws and institutions should be designed to cultivate virtue. The legislator must ensure that administrators are themselves worthy, and education produces virtuous citizens.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose of legislation: prioritize peace, safety, and rest over conquest
rubrics_metrics.description: A legislator's care should be to render the people fit for defence so they are not enslaved, to secure the safety of subjects, and not to make conquest or extensive command the supreme object. Training citizens primarily for war to enslave others is a mistaken aim for a legislator.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: States trained primarily for conquest may gain power but are not thereby happy; the legislator ought to inculcate the ability to be at rest and enjoy peace. Only those fit to be slaves should be slaves; laws should aim at justice and the safety of citizens rather than empire-building.

rubrics_metrics.name: Core civic virtues required for a happy state
rubrics_metrics.description: A city must be temperate, brave, and patient; bravery and patience are necessary for labour and resisting attack; philosophy (theoretical deliberation), temperance and justice are important for rest and peace; greater leisure requires greater philosophy and self-restraint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Different virtues are needed in war and peace: war engenders courage and some justice, but peace and abundance risk luxury and insolence, so temperance and justice must be cultivated especially in times of rest. The legislator's education program should promote these virtues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citizen education: harmonise nature, custom, and reason; fit education to roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Men become good by nature, custom, and reason. Education must address both parts of the soul (reasoning and non-reasoning) and their associated habits (intellect and appetite). Governors and governed should share some education but differ in others; one ought to 'first learn to obey' before commanding. Education should tend toward rest and peace, and cultivate the superior parts of the soul.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Educative programs must be staged by age and role: some training is common to all, other instruction specialized (e.g., training that cultivates courage for youth and judgment for elders). Custom can correct errors of reason, so institutions should align habituation with rational ends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Family law and reproductive/childbearing regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislator should regulate matrimony timing and conditions to secure bodies of children fit to the city's aims: avoid too early marriages (produce small, ill-framed offspring and maternal mortality) and too late marriages (parents too old to benefit from children's assistance). Recommended ages: woman ~18, man ~37 (approximately), with appropriate seasonality (winter) and observance of medical/naturalist precepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intergenerational spacing should neither be too large nor too small so that parents and children can properly perform reciprocal duties and maintain reverence. The body of the child and parental bodily constitution should be considered; children should have habits of labour suited to freemen (moderate labour, not specialised extreme training).

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing and priority in education: body before soul; appetites before reason
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the body and the non-reasoning part of the soul (appetite, anger, desire) are developed before the reasoning part, the legislator's first attention must be to perfecting the bodies of children, then to the appetites, and finally to the mind/reason.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical implication: physical training, health, and habit-formation must precede formal intellectual instruction. The curriculum should reflect developmental order, ensuring bodily fitness and regulated appetites before cultivating theoretical intelligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political participation and rotation of rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Although it would be better if governors always governed and others always obeyed (if naturally superior), equality and justice mean many states must have citizens both govern and be governed in turn: 'it is just that those who are equal should have everything alike.' Yet governors ought to excel the governed; the legislator must contrive systems so all have their equal share in administration while ensuring governors' excellence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should balance permanence and rotation to avoid unrest and innovation from dissatisfied groups. Education should make those who govern demonstrably superior in relevant virtues, but legal structures should allow shared participation to maintain stability and justice.
